what: Evenhand is a two-joint arm in the vertical plane. Motor A turns the shoulder, motor B the elbow. Behind each joint, ordinary stock parts act as counterweights: they balance the upper arm about the shoulder and the forearm about the elbow. The program visits nine poses, every combination of shoulder −20°, 0°, +20° and elbow −30°, 0°, +30°, holds each for 1.2 s and returns home. In the simulator both motors hold every pose with almost no torque: the shoulder needs about 0.35 mN·m and the elbow less than 0.01 mN·m.
try: In Robot Lab, choose File → Open a model… and open evenhand.ldr. Put programs/evenhand.bw in the Code tab, choose ⇦ To blocks and press Robot Lab's Run button, which connects the virtual SPIKE hub.
Watch the counterweights during the nine poses: as each link tips down on one side, its counterweight rises on the other.
Use the manual controls (shoulder ±20°, elbow ±30°) and let go at any pose: the balanced arm has no tendency to fall back.
Then open evenhand-control.ldr, where the forearm weights sit closer to the elbow, and run the same program. Reload the complete scene before each comparison.
why: Gravity pulls on every part of a link. About its joint, the parts in front and behind produce opposite torques. When the counterweight's mass times its distance behind the joint equals the link's mass times the distance of its own centre of mass in front, the torques cancel at every angle, because both scale with the cosine of the same angle. A balanced arm therefore needs motor torque only to accelerate, not to hold still.
matters: Desk lamps, robot arms, cranes, lift bridges and lift doors use counterweights or springs for the same reason: the motor or the person only has to move the load, not to carry it.
question: Why does the balanced arm need almost no holding torque at every pose, not just when the arm is level?
answer: Because the link's weight torque and the counterweight's torque both change with the cosine of the link's angle. If they cancel when level, they cancel at every angle. The small remaining shoulder torque, about 0.35 mN·m, shows the balance is not perfect but is more than ten times smaller than in the control.
further: Use m₁·d₁ = m₂·d₂ to estimate how far behind the elbow the forearm weights must sit to balance the forearm.
Why must the shoulder counterweight balance the elbow motor and the forearm with its counterweights as well as the upper arm?
Look up how a balanced desk lamp uses springs instead of weights.
formula: Holding torque about a joint: τ = g·cos(φ)·Σ mᵢ·dᵢ (dᵢ signed distance along the link). Balanced when Σ mᵢ·dᵢ = 0, so τ = 0 for every φ.
